title: Review of unmanned ground vehicles for PV plant inspection
abstract: The growth of utility-scale solar power plants, which can now have more than a million PV modules, has created the need for automated monitoring and inspection technologies. Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAVs, or “drones”) have become widely used, especially for thermal infrared imaging, due to their falling cost, increasing technical capability, and ability to survey many modules quickly. However drones have certain limitations: they do not see the underside of PV arrays or balance-of-system equipment, it is difficult to hold a steady position for long- or repeated-exposure imaging, and operating permits can be onerous. In such cases unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs, or “robots”) can be advantageous for PV plant inspection. This paper reviews robot movement mechanisms (wheels, tracks and legs), types of PV faults for which they are suited, and their current status of use in commercial solar farms. Further, it examines typical obstacles to robot navigation in Australian solar farms. Key conclusions are that robots are likely to complement rather than replace drones for PV inspection, and are especially valuable for reducing fire risk by detecting hot-spots in electrical components.

## **1. Introduction**

There are strong motivations for automating the inspection of solar photovoltaic (PV) power plants: Sites have become very large and can have more than a million PV modules; minimising the number of inspection workers increases safety and reduces cost; and advances in autonomous vehicles and computer vision have made it technically and economically feasible.

So far unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs, referred to as “drones” in this report) have been the main platform for automating PV plant inspection; the technology is briefly reviewed in the next section. In comparison the use of unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs, or “robots”) in solar farms is less common and the technology less mature. A detailed technoeconomic comparison and discussion of robots relative to drones is presented in Section 6; below we note key tasks and situations in which drones are constrained:

- Use of drones is restricted or banned in many places [1]. Where allowed, it is a common requirement that the operator keeps visual line of sight of the drone which limits its range

- They require a skilled operator (autonomous drone flight is technically feasible but rarely permitted). Piloting an industrial drone requires significant training and a licence, hence availability of pilots is a common bottleneck

- They do not “see” the back-side of PV modules or balance-of-system (BOS) components beneath modules such as cables and connectors

- In moderate wind it is difficult to maintain a stationary airborne position for long-exposure or multiple-exposure imaging. In strong wind drones cannot be flown at all

- In usual practice they do not take close-up images of PV modules, as it is desirable to fly at a sufficient distance for safety and to image a large number of modules in each flight [2]

- Their payload weight is limited

- Their flight time is relatively short, in the region of a half hour [3]. As a result regular battery swaps are needed which reduces operational efficiency

- Aerial infrared (IR) images of PV modules can be distorted by reflections from the modules of the sun, clouds and surrounding landscape [4].

Robots are generally free from these constraints. In particular, they have a good view of electrical components such as PV cables, connectors (MC4), combiner boxes, inverters, switches and breakers (Fig. 1). It is these items that are most at risk of overheating or arcing and causing a fire; PV modules themselves rarely originate fires [5]. Further, the risk of fire increases if vegetation grows around electrical equipment, which can only be seen from the ground. Hence automatic thermal (IR) imaging is an especially strong motivation for using robots to inspect solar

Apart from thermal anomalies, issues with PV systems that are suited to ground-level observation include the following. Many of these issues can be observed by drones, but robots have a better vantage point.

- module backsheets — degradation, damage, burn marks

- module rear glass — cracks

- mechanical faults, e.g. dangling PV cables, damaged connectors, loose module clamps

- rusting or damaged racks and trackers

- soiling on the rear side of modules (not common but can occur)

- high vegetation

- bird nests and animal infestation

- pooling water and mud

- soil erosion.

This paper reviews the use of robots for PV plant inspection, focusing on: (i) the status of market adoption (as of mid 2024), (ii) applicable inspection tools and methods, and (iii) physical obstacles to robot movement in solar farms, particularly in Australia.

## **2. Drone inspection**

It has been estimated that using drones to collect images of solar farms is faster than manual, ground-based methods by a factor of ten to twenty [4,8,9]. This efficiency, coupled with falling costs and increasing performance, has meant that drones have become widely used by researchers and industry for surveying PV installations.

Several reviews of aircraft and drone inspection technology for PV plants have been published [4,8,10–12]. In this summary, we focus on PV imaging techniques that have been deployed aerially, i.e. nonimaging inspection methods such as performance data analysis and I-V traces are outside the present scope.

The most advanced imaging tools are visual and thermal IR cameras. IR camera manufacturers sell light-weight devices specifically designed for drones, and drone manufacturers have started selling units integrated with an IR camera “out of the box”. Visual images can identify mechanical faults such as broken front glass and delamination of modules, as well as operation and maintenance (O&M) issues such as soiling and high weeds. Thermal IR images reveal issues that have thermal signatures such as module hot-spots, potential-induced degradation, and disconnected or shunted groups of cells or modules [4,10–12].

Drone imaging of PV plants is not simple, however. IR images are sensitive to environmental conditions (e.g. irradiation and wind), the

operating state of PV strings, and how the drone and camera are operated [2,4]. Obtaining high-quality aerial IR images that can be reliably interpreted requires precise and consistent methods. Because of these challenges, the IEA-PVPS report of 2022 [12] noted that aerial IR imaging was not yet a “turnkey solution”. However in mid-2024 we interviewed two major international PV plant developers/operators who informed that there are now several companies providing IR drone surveys and fault reports, per IEC Technical Specification 62446–3, as a fully commercial service. Both developers said they use such services annually and additionally after severe storms, at certain sites.

Several further imaging technologies are in the research and development stage. Drone-based electroluminescence (EL) imaging has also been demonstrated experimentally [8]. However it typically needs to be performed at night with dedicated hardware to inject current to the modules [9,12]. Ultraviolet fluorescence (UVF) imaging provides information on the condition of modules’ encapsulant due to cracks and ageing. It requires illumination with particular light wavelengths in otherwise dark conditions; it too has been deployed on drones experimentally but not yet adopted commercially [8,12].

Photoluminescence (PL) examines near-infrared (NIR) radiation around 1150 nm, emitted by recombination of electrons and holes in silicon devices [13]. The quality of PV material is related to its luminosity in this wavelength range: brighter pixels in PL images correspond to higher implied voltage in that part of the device [14]. This reveals cracks, degraded and inactive parts of modules [8,15]. In recent years daylight photoluminescence (DPL) imaging has been developed using sunlight as the light source [16,17], allowing measurement of PV systems in the field during daytime. Recently Weber et al [18] demonstrated DPL imaging from a drone via “contactless modulation”, in which the PV system’s inverter is used to switch between open- and closed-circuit operation, which avoids the need for dedicated hardware to be connected to the modules. Because DPL can be performed during the day, without connecting additional hardware, and be deployed by drone, it is seem as a promising PV inspection technology.

## **3. Robots for PV plant inspection**

Autonomous robot platforms and computer-vision technology have advanced greatly in recent years, and many commercial robots have been introduced for inspecting indoor and outdoor industrial facilities [3]. In this section we focus on robotic inspection of equipment at industrial facilities in general, not just solar farms, and exclude other tasks that can be performed by robots such as intruder surveillance and product quality control [19]. Development of autonomous inspection

robots has largely been an engineering exercise built upon scientific advances in computer vision, positioning and navigation algorithms, and locomotion control, which reflected in the organisation of this section.

## _3.1. Locomotion types_

The three main types of robot locomotion are wheels, tracks, and legs [20]. These are not rigid categories and hybrids exist between these, for example: The “feet” on a legged robot can be replaced by wheels, providing fast movement on paved surfaces and agility when obstacles are encountered. Middle ground between tracks and wheels can be achieved by increasing the number of wheels on a robot, especially driven wheels. A combined drone/robot system has even been developed [21]. Other niche locomotion types also exist, for example snakelike motion and wall climbing, but are outside the present scope.

Each locomotion type has advantages and limitations, making them suitable for different environments and purposes [3]. A qualitative comparison of features relevant to PV plant inspection is presented in Table 1 , based on specifications of robots in the marketplace that we surveyed in mid 2024, and a 2012 report by Bruzzone & Quaglia [20]. Cost is omitted from the table because we found an enormous range in the market within each type of locomotion, and costs can change quickly, so it is impossible to generalize on this feature.

The notable feature of legged robots is their great agility, in particular their ability to navigate steps, stairs, and other high obstacles. While this is valuable for indoor inspection tasks, it is less relevant to solar farms as steps are uncommon in the field. Industrial legged robots tend to be expensive (e.g. Boston Dynamic’s Spot model [22] exceeds $100,000), although inexpensive consumer-grade models have become available (e.g. the Unitree Go2 base model is advertised at $2800 [23] as at mid-2024). Other drawbacks of legged locomotion are relatively low speed and efficiency, and high complexity which tends to disadvantage operating cost and reliability. This review did not consider humanoid robots as they have not so far been used for industrial inspection, however we briefly note that robot manufacturers are making rapid progress on their development and we speculate that this application might occur in future.

Tracks create a large contact area with the ground, spreading the weight of the robot and providing much grip. This makes them ideal for heavy payloads, soft or loose soil, and steep inclines. However the deliberate increase in friction with the ground tends to penalise energy efficiency and speed. They are available as bare platforms (e.g. Robodyne MaxxII model [24]) to which the user attaches their own devices.

Wheels are simple, low cost, energy efficient, and accept heavy payloads. Their main drawback is their need for relatively flat and firm ground. This can be mitigated by using larger or wider wheels and more powerful motors, although of course this increases cost and energy use. Wheeled robots are also widely available as development platforms (e.g. Clearpath Robotics Husky model [25]).

We searched for commercially-available inspection robots in mid2024. We found 36 models, and noted that the market is growing rapidly with new models being launched every few months. The types of locomotion employed were quite evenly distributed: Of the 36 models surveyed, 13 had legs, 10 had wheels, 1 was a hybrid of legs and wheels,

Interestingly, none of the 36 models use articulated wheels, in which wheels are mounted to an arm that can passively rotate (e.g. NASA Curiosity rover). ## _3.2. Navigation technologies_

The effectiveness of autonomous field robots relies on motion planning and control. In recent years robot navigation and obstacle avoidance capabilities have advanced greatly, largely due to improved control algorithms, advanced sensors and modern cameras. Control techniques have been developed to ensure precise path planning, particularly for both kinematic and dynamic models of robots. Studies [27–32] have introduced model predictive control methods, which enable robots to accurately navigate in the presence of disturbances while adhering to operational constraints. Advances in reliability of navigation include the so-called “sliding mode” control [33] and Lyapunov stability method [34]. To achieve robust control particularly in handling disturbances, slip, or skid in vehicles, various types of “observers” (algorithms that interpret data from the robot’s multiple sensors) have been designed. These include the extended Kalman filter [33], unknown input observers [34], and extended state observers [35], which are used to estimate parameters such as orientation, velocity, and external disturbances.

Most research to date on autonomous navigation of PV plants has naturally focused on aerial drones, where the key goal is efficient path planning rather than obstacle avoidance. For drones, the most widelyadopted method is vision-based control, which identifies PV rows by detecting module edges to automatically generate flight paths [36–40]. An automated system was proposed by De Benedetti et al [39] that integrates drones and robots for inspection, focusing on path planning for autonomous drones and trajectory tracking for robots. However, the system did not address collision avoidance.

Regarding robot navigation for PV inspection, Hayajneh and Al Mahasneha [41] proposed a backstepping control approach for path planning employing GPS and inertial measurement unit (IMU) data. The system estimated vehicle velocity and position through an observer, with feedback to the controller to improve accuracy. The Husky robot (see section 3.4) uses autonomous navigation software developed by the robot’s manufacturer and RTK-GPS sensors, which in ideal conditions give positional accuracy of 14 mm. Additionally, the robot uses LiDAR and depth cameras for obstacle detection. An alternative to RTK-GPS is differential GPS, which is employed by the MAINBOT experimental PV inspection robot [42]. These approaches capture the main navigation instruments available for autonomous PV inspection, in particular differential- or RTK-GPS, IMU, LiDAR, and cameras. Although these instruments are widely available “off the shelf”, it is challenging to integrate and deploy them reliably, and at very large solar farms there are communication limits discussed in the next section.

## _3.3. Communication technologies_

It is usual for field inspection robots to communicate in real-time with a “mission control” base, where a human operator controls or simply monitors the robot, depending on its degree of autonomy. One PV inspection robot in the market, the Antecursor II (see section 3.4), is designed to operate with zero human involvement, yet it too always maintains live contact with a base in case errors or incidents occur. Communication is necessarily two-way: robots typically broadcast their position, status, and possibly live video to a base station, while the base sends the robot any required control instructions and — if high-precision GPS-RTK or differential-GPS is implemented — also position correction

data. The main technologies by which field robots and base stations communicate include the following:

WiFi — Many inspection robots are supplied with built-in WiFi, standards family IEEE 802.11, a type of radio communication, as it is widely used and easy to implement. WiFi enables direct communication between robot and base station via a common wireless local-area network, as well as internet access for the robot, assuming the access point is connected to the internet, which can be useful for some applications. A major downside to WiFi is the allowable distance from the access point or router, which is typically tens of meters, and at most hundreds of meters for high-specification equipment in ideal outdoor conditions [43]. This is sufficient for inspection robots at indoor facilities with extensive WiFi coverage, but is not suited to solar farms where the robot may be kilometres from the access point. Also, conventional routers are not designed to withstand outdoor conditions, although rugged commercial models are available.

Radio — Radio frequency (RF) technology allows direct radio communication over long distances, albeit at relatively low data speeds. Robot and base station each have an RF transceiver (transmitter + receiver). Many such units are available which operate over distances of kilometres, even up to 20 km when directional antenna are used [44]. There is typically a trade-off between range and bandwidth, for example a long-range radio (LoRa) unit with range over 10 km may have bandwidth less than 300 kbps. Hence data-intensive functions, such as live video streaming from the robot, are challenging for RF in solar farm inspections. It is interesting that live video streaming is common for drones, yet none of the PV inspection robots in our survey (section 3.4) were supplied off-the-shelf with RF communication.

Mobile (Cellular) — Inspection robots can be equipped with an electronic module or USB device which provides Internet connection via a mobile phone network (LTE, 4G, or 5G). Software on the robot makes it appear as a device on the same local network as the base station. High data speeds are possible, depending on the network specification and signal strength. Naturally the solar farm must have mobile phone reception for this approach, which is a significant drawback as they are often located in remote areas with poor or no mobile coverage.

Satellite — For Internet connectivity in areas without mobile phone coverage, a satellite Internet service is technically a possibility. Its main

disadvantage is its relatively high cost, currently in the order of $100 per month. It is the built-in communication technology for the Antecursor II PV inspection robot (section 3.4) via the StarLink service, however no other examples of satellite use by commercial outdoor inspection robots were found.

## _3.4. Market status of PV inspection robots_

As of mid 2024, we found six commercial ground robots that were systematically used for PV plant monitoring (Fig. 2). Some were specifically designed for this task, while others were general-purpose platforms that were adapted for it. Other robots have been trialled in solar farm inspections but were excluded from this list as they appeared to be one-off events, i.e. not systematic use. It appears that all of the six units are going through “proof of performance” field trials, but from available online data and discussions with PV plant operators we understand that none are being used in standard operations at solar farms. An overview of the robots is provided below, roughly in order of technical and commercial maturity.

- a) Husky Observer – Clearpath Robotics of Canada produces a portfolio of wheeled robots, its Husky Observer unit is designed for inspection of outdoor sites [45]. The company can integrate and configure sensors requested by the user, including a pan/tilt/zoom (PTZ) IR camera, and has supplied several units specifically for PV plant inspection. It has a highly-developed user interface which allows the operator to set autonomous navigation routes or remotely pilot the robot. Route following is achieved via GPS-RTK, and obstacle avoidance via 3D LiDAR and two depth cameras. The system does not analyze collected images to detect or characterize faults. A docking station is available for automatic recharging. The company was recently purchased by Rockwell Automation, which makes the Husky the only robot in this list which is supplied by a large and established corporation.

- b) OnSight – A tracked robot manufactured by OnSight Technology, a US computer-vision company [46]. It was designed specifically to facilitate PV plant maintenance: The robot has IR and visual cameras, and the company claims its software can autonomously identify

- d) Boston Dynamics Spot – The company s quadruped, dog-like robots received widespread attention when launched in the early 2000 s. Its current Spot model is designed for automated inspection of indoor and outdoor industrial facilities [22]. It can be optionally equipped with an IR camera and generate automatic reports of hot subject areas, but it does so generically, not specifically for PV systems. Normally it is remotely piloted by a human as it has no native localisation tool such as GPS, and uses LiDAR for obstacle avoidance and mapping its immediate surroundings. A press report of its use in a Chile PV plant [52] described it as “following a programmed route”, but the degree of autonomy was not clear. A docking station is available for automatic recharging, and the manufacturer’s software can control and manage a fleet of the robots.

- e) Leapting – Leapting is a Chinese company that mainly produces automated PV cleaning machines [53]. It launched a PV inspection robot with tracks in 2023 [54,55]. The robot can autonomously follow a predefined route, however it does not have LiDAR and its obstacle avoidance capability was not stated. The robot is equipped with visual and IR cameras on a PTZ mounting. It analyses images to automatically identify PV faults including cracks, hot spots, soiling and animal infestation. The company said it has been deployed at one client PV site as of January 2024.

- f) S4 – Manufactured by SMP Robotics in the US, which primarily produces wheeled robots for site security and surveillance. Its S4 model is equipped with an IR camera. The company states the robot can “cruis[e] automatically between the rows of solar panels” and send an alarm if it detects abnormal temperatures [56]. It does not appear that specific PV faults are identified. No information was available on its use in PV plants so far.

In summary, three companies were identified that produce dedicated IR inspection robots for PV plants on a commercial basis, all of which use tracks. A fourth produces a general-purpose wheeled robot which has been configured and used for this task for several customers. Another two companies state their robots are usable for PV inspection, but from available literature they do not appear highly adapted for it. All six are essentially undergoing field testing, either internally or by customers, and ongoing development.

Overall the market status of PV inspection robots can be considered “near-commercial”. Proof-of-concept has been achieved, and proof-ofperformance is underway. Technical performance, reliability, and economics are yet to be validated through full-scale and long-term use. There is room for further technology development in autonomous routeplanning and navigation, as well as PV fault detection and characterisation. Like the aerial IR survey industry, specialist firms might own the robots and perform site inspections as a service, rather than PV plant owners acquiring and operating robots themselves.

## **4. Imaging technologies and Practices**

## _4.1. Perspective and distance_

Being on the ground creates opportunities and challenges for how robots obtain images during PV plant inspections. Ideally, images of PV modules are taken from an approximately perpendicular angle, and capture whole module(s) in the image. This is straightforward for aerial drones but difficult for ground robots. Particularly difficult situations include:

- (i) When modules are at low tilt angle, e.g. for PV systems with fixed mountings at low latitudes, or PV systems with trackers near “see” the

- noon. This situation makes it difficult for the robot to front side of modules. To see the back side of modules, the robot would need to position itself directly beneath them and point cameras upward, which is technically challenging and driving beneath arrays is risky. Possible solutions include: conducting inspections of tracked PV systems in the morning or afternoon; manually setting the tracker tilt to a steep angle during inspection; or mounting cameras on a tall pole attached to the robot as with the Antecursor II.

- (ii) If PV rows are closely spaced or the camera’s field of view is narrow, whole modules may not fit in the frame and images must be stitched together. Also, if the robot is closer to modules than the camera’s minimum focus distance, images will be blurred. These perspective issues are discussed further below.

- (iii) Some PV installations have insufficient space for robots to drive around them, such as “tent” mounting (Fig. 3), agri-PV systems in which there are crops below and around the PV, and of course roof and floating PV systems. On the other hand vertical PV systems, which are increasingly used in grazing farmland, appear ideally suited to ground-level robot inspection because of their orientation (Fig. 4), and for the same are difficult to image by aerial drones.

We consider in further detail the perspective and distance for ground-based imaging of PV systems. As mentioned the usual goals are to: capture entire modules in an image, which makes image analysis easier than stitching together images of parts of a module; obtain a roughly perpendicular viewing angle; and of course ensure the subject is in focus. The relevant factors that determine these include distance between camera and module, size and orientation of modules, and the camera/lens field of view (FOV) angle and minimum focus distance (MFD). We gathered typical values of these factors at solar farms and estimated whether the mentioned goals could be achieved readily and simultaneously.

**Fig. 4.** For vertical PV systems, ground robots have a better viewing angle than aerial drones [58].

- Module orientation and spacing: Six solar farms in Western Australia were surveyed. It was found that five used 1P configuration (modules mounted on single-axis trackers in portrait orientation, one module across) and one used 2P (two modules across). The average 1P row spacing was 6.0 m, the minimum was 5.0 m, and the sole 2P spacing was 9.1 _m_ .

- Module size: At present modules for utility-scale PV plants are –

- commonly around 2.0 2.1 m long and 1.0 m wide, although modules up to 2.4 m long are becoming more common

- Camera/lens characteristics: A range of lenses is available for many industrial IR cameras, for example the Teledyne FLIR Boson camera can be ordered with seven lenses ranging from 6[◦] to 95[◦] FOV. The advantage of wide FOV is capturing whole modules or several modules in an image, the drawback is reduced resolution (pixels per subject area) and increased barrel distortion. Around 32[◦] FOV is midrange, and often used for IR camera models that are available with only a single lens. MFD depends on the specific camera and lens and data is not always readily available. For the example of the Boson 32[◦] FOV lens, which can be considered a mid-range configuration, the MFD is 3 m. Lenses with wider FOV have shorter MFD, i.e. the goal of capturing whole modules aligns with the goal of maintaining focus at short distances.

Assuming 1P layout, 2.1 m module length, 6 m row spacing, and the robot driving mid-way between rows, then the camera needs to image an object 2.1 m long from a distance of 3 m. Therefore from trigonometry the camera’s FOV needs to be 38.6[◦] or wider. (This is a simplistic analysis ignoring factors such as module tilt and camera orientation and alignment). For 2P layout and 9.1 m row spacing, the critical FOV is 49.6[◦] . Using the above data for the FLIR Boson IR camera, a lens with 32[◦] FOV would give a minimum focus distance around 3 m, which is just adequate for a robot driving mid-way between 1P rows. If the rows were spaced any more tightly, the robot would be so close to modules that they would be out of focus, or it would need to drive off the centreline.

The worst case scenario encountered, namely 1P layout with 5.0 m spacing and 2.4 m long modules, would require a FOV of 51.3[◦] . These FOVs are catered for by certain IR camera models for which a sufficiently wide lenses are available, but IR cameras with a “normal” FOV, around 30[◦] , may not capture images of whole modules. Normal or wider FOV lenses will capture in-focus images if the robot travels mid-way between rows, but the minimum focal distance, which is typically greater than a meter, might prevent approaching objects for close-up imaging.

Essentially, the trade-off is between lens focal length and image resolution: wider lenses can capture whole modules and remain in focus at closer distances, but sacrifice resolution, i.e. pixels per subject area. This trade-off could be avoided by zoom lenses for IR cameras — both wide-angle and zoomed-in images could be obtained from the same robot position. Such lenses have recently been announced [59].

## _4.2. O&M technologies for robots_

In this section, sensors and other hardware for PV inspection robots are discussed and proposed.

Visual and thermal IR cameras can be considered standard devices for PV inspection in the field. Their use in aerial drones is already common practice, and they are deployed on all six of the commercial PV inspection robots described in section 3.4. Given that robots have greater payload and battery capacities than drones, one may expect that robots would be equipped with with larger, heavier, and higherspecification cameras, for example actively-cooled microbolometer detectors for high-performance medium- and long-wave IR cameras. However in practice drone cameras have advanced to the point that there is little difference in their specification compared to those used for inspection robots. For both, typical visual image resolution is around 50 MP, and long-wave IR resolution 640 × 512 pixels.

Although drones and robots use similar types of visual cameras, robots tend to use more of them. Robots use multiple cameras primarily for navigation and obstacle avoidance, but they can also be repurposed for obtaining additional views for inspection. High-performance IR cameras are expensive, above $10,000, and no examples of multiple IR cameras on an autonomous inspection vehicle (robot or drone) were found. As seen in Fig. 2, several PV inspection robots mount the primary cameras on pan-tilt gimbals so the operator can focus on subjects of interest. Inexpensive low resolution, wide angle IR cameras are available (e.g. FLIR Lepton with 160 × 120 resolution, 57[◦] FOV, low $100 s). The authors have trialled a variety of commercial IR cameras and note that wide-angle resolution devices are useful for quickly surveying a large area of a solar farm in low detail, while high-performance cameras are useful for examining specific equipment in high detail. We propose that they be deployed in tandem: using a wide-angle camera to detect thermal anomalies in a broad image of a solar farm, and then investigate those anomalies in detail with a high high-resolution, narrow-angle IR camera on a pan-tilt mounting or by approaching closely with the robot vehicle.

Outdoor electroluminescence (EL) and daytime photoluminescence (DPL) imaging via drones were discussed in section 3. As DPL can, in some implementations, be performed without additional hardware being connected to PV modules or illuminating them, it is especially promising for autonomous field inspection. As mentioned researchers have already deployed such a DPL system on a drone, so in principle it should also be possible on a ground robot. An advantage of doing so would be that the camera would be maintained in stable position during repeated exposures — which is difficult to achieve by drone — reducing the need for post-processing of images, particularly registration alignment), noting that multiple raw images are required to produce each final DPL image. Performing both IR and DPL inspection of a solar farm would be attractive as they are complementary: IR especially detects faults with electrical pathways and components in PV devices, while DPL provides information on PV cell quality and degradation.

A robot platform for autonomous PV plant inspection is a significant cost, therefore it is economically attractive to maximise its capabilities, i.e. adding sensors and tools to a robot increases its total package cost by a small proportion. As well as enhancing inspection capabilities, it would be attractive for the robot to perform other site operation and maintenance (O&M) tasks. Security monitoring, for example, would be relatively simple to implement as the robot is already equipped with the required cameras; detecting intruders becomes a matter of route programming and image analysis. Indeed the manufacturer of the S4 thermal inspection robot (section 3.4) principally develops security-oriented models. Another field task which has been facilitated by PV inspection robots is module inventory management, where barcodes or serial numbers of installed modules are automatically read and recorded, which is useful for construction validation and warranty purposes [60].

Weed trimming is another common O&M task for solar farms, and as mentioned a mower has been incorporated into the Antecursor II

inspection robot. We propose that the reverse could also be achieved, i.e. adding visual and IR cameras to an existing mowing machine, removing the need for a dedicated inspection robot altogether. Tractors are presently used at some solar farms to deploy PV cleaning machines or mowing sleds, to which inspection cameras might be added. In the case of cleaning machines, care would need to be taken to ensure that the cleaning head does not shade the modules being imaged, or others in the same string, as the shadow would interfere with the string’s electrical operation and thus thermal appearance [61]. This concern may also hinder adding IR cameras to PV cleaning robots that run along modules themselves.

## **5. Ground conditions of PV plants**

Using ground robots for PV plant inspection obviously requires that they can physically traverse the site. Challenges may be environmental, such as soft sand and thick vegetation, as well as man-made such linkage bars between tracker rows. Also, the terrain will influence the type of robot locomotion required. In this section we consider ground conditions of PV plants for robotic inspection, especially in Australia.

## _5.1. Types of obstacles_

Many factors can impact the ability of ground robots to traverse and survey a PV site, which are grouped and discussed as follows. Natural features **—**

Natural impediments include steeply inclined land, soft sand, rocks, ditches, tall or thick vegetation, and pools of water and mud. When such hindrances are extensive or severe it may be necessary to use tracks for robot locomotion, which are adept at coping with rough or loose terrain. Indeed as noted in the previous section, so far most robots developed specifically for PV plant inspection use tracks. However in many solar farms the ground is cleared and graded during construction, and kept clear as part of regular maintenance, in which case wheeled robots may be sufficient. The terrain of solar farms is unlikely to be so rough as to require the agility of a legged robot.

Both tracked and wheeled robots can be engineered to cope with more difficult terrain by increasing their mechanical specifications (e.g. power and dimensions) and also their intelligence (e.g. using computer vision to drive around a shrub rather than over it). As noted above, wheeled robots could potentially cope with rougher terrain by attaching the wheels to articulated arms.

— PV system layout

A major potential obstacle for robotic PV plant inspection is the presence of linkage bars between PV rows, used in some models of horizontal single-axis trackers (Fig. 5). Although relatively uncommon at solar farms, such bars are employed in tracker models from several major manufacturers (e.g. Array Technologies, Trina Agile-1P, Soltec SFOneX, PVH AxoneDuo). Typically positioned tens of centimetres above ground, the bars prevent wheeled and tracked robots and also regular maintenance vehicles from driving between rows. In such cases the robot would need to “double back” on itself in each row, adding length and complexity to its route.

## _5.2. Australia_

The preceding section reviewed generic obstacles faced by robots traversing solar farms. Here we present a survey of ground conditions at a number of PV sites in Australia. The survey was conducted by visiting six solar farms and interviewing industry professionals in the Australian PV O& M sector. Specific sites visited in the survey are anonymised for commercial confidentiality, but were mainly in rural areas outside of Perth, in the south-west of the country, and Sydney in the east. Interviewees provided information on solar farms in additional parts of the country.

Australia’s climate zones and rainfall are shown in Fig. 7, and the location of large PV plants in Fig. 8. Central Australia is arid, but most solar farms are located in populated regions of the east, south-east and south-west coasts. As shown in Fig. 7 the rainy season varies with latitude, however the salient point is that almost all Australian solar farms can expect moderate to heavy rain at some time of year.

A variety of obstacles to robot movement at solar farms was identified in the survey, as follows. Vegetation was an issue for all solar farms investigated (Fig. 9(a)). Mowing was generally conducted ad-hoc, i.e. – only when required. Moderate weeds, 20 30 cm high, were common in farmland regions (b), which we expect mid-sized robots could drive over. However tall weeds, over half a meter, were sometimes observed (c) that would likely prevent use of even a tracked robot. It is difficult for a mower to reach all the way under PV arrays, and high weeds remained

We had anticipated that rocks and boulders would be an obstacle at some sites, however we did not observe any, possibly because they were removed during site preparation and construction. An interviewee advised that locations with very rocky terrain or prone to persistent flooding would be unlikely to be selected for a PV plant in the first place.

A key observation from the survey is that there is no such thing as “the” ground condition of a PV site, rather conditions change throughout the year with the weather — particularly rain —and vegetation. For example, it was reported by interviewees that some solar farms in Australia’s east are readily navigable for much of the year but pools of water and mud form during the rainy season. In the south-west, vegetation grows quickly in winter but dies off in summer. This suggests that operating PV inspection robots on a fixed schedule may be difficult; having the flexibility to perform inspections when conditions are favourable, e.g. after mowing and no recent rain, would be advantageous, and even necessary at some locations.

Overall the survey of ground conditions of Australian solar farms found that the most common obstacles to robots were vegetation and pools of water or mud. There were also site-specific but severe obstacles such as deep ditches from soil erosion, linkage bars between tracker rows and near-ground cable trays.

The findings suggests that simple wheeled inspection robots could be used at most sites, provided vegetation is kept short and the ground is dry during inspection. Sites with rough terrain, fast-growing vegetation or persistent mud may require a tracked robot. To some extent, if an ordinary maintenance vehicle can traverse a solar farm, it should be possible for a robot of moderate size and power to do the same. As robots gain more sophisticated computer-vision and navigation algorithms, they will cope with more difficult terrain by driving around isolated obstacles such as shrubs and puddles. However sites with “hard”

physical barriers such as tracker linkage bars or cable trays appear unsuited to automated ground inspection, as they would require inefficient routes or perhaps very agile legged robots which have drawbacks discussed in section 4.

## _5.3. Global_

Outside Australia, the variety of solar farm terrains is as wide as the world’s range of climates and geographies, and it is beyond the scope of this paper to characterise PV terrains globally. However studies of PV site selection criteria offer useful insights. Uyan [66] and Sanchez-Loz- ́ ano et al [67] noted the growing use of geographic information systems (GIS) to evaluate terrain as part of the process for selecting sites for solar farms, especially their slope and vegetation which are important to robot deployment. The study used a maximum ground slope of 3 % as a criterion for site selection. A review by Merrouni et al [68] found six solar farm slope criteria in the literature, ranging from 1 % to 7 %, although that upper value was an outlier: the other five cited cases were 4 % or less, and the authors settled on a slope limit of 5 %. A 10 % limit was adopted by Yushchenko et al [69] for a similar study in West Africa, and 5 % by Finn & McKenzie [70] in Northern Ireland. Assuming a midrange value of 5 % maximum allowed ground slope, this is within the section 3.4. specifications of all robots reviewed in

The literature also provides some consideration of solar farm vegetation. In an assessment of potential solar farm sites in Serbia, Doljak & Stanojevic [71] permitted pastures and tree-free natural terrains (e.g. shrubs, grasses, and sparsely vegetated areas), but ruled out forests and very wet areas. The mentioned review by Merrouni et al focused on Morocco’s arid areas, which have little vegetation. Finn and McKenzie’s analysis used sophisticated satellite images to classify land cover, and favoured grasslands, heath, and farm land in that order (forests were ruled out). Yilmaz et al [72] specifically considered the risk of floods and soil erosion as a result of heavy rains, which they noted are important

yet often overlooked criteria for PV site evaluation.

The key insight from these studies is that solar farms are often proposed only on land that is reasonably flat and sparsely vegetated or already used for farming. Prima facie, such terrain would also be amenable to use of ground robots. Of course individual sites may present their own obstacles: As well as those observed in Australia, namely uncontrolled vegetation, pools of water/mud, and tracker linkage bars, challenges from the local climate and geography may arise such as snow, soft sand, ditches and rocks.

The key advantage of robots relative to drones is their ability to inspect the rear-side of PV modules and balance-of-system (BOS) equipment beneath them. As noted, this is especially important for solar farm safety as electrical parts such as PV connectors, cables and breakers are the principal sources of fires. Fire risk is heightened when vegetation grows around electrical equipment, which robots are also well placed to detect. Industry sources interviewed for this study said that thermal inspection of BOS equipment is a near-essential O&M task for solar farms.

Of course aerial drones have their own advantages. They are well suited to detecting faulty modules in a solar farm, and they are very efficient, able to survey an entire solar farm in hours. Drone inspection technology is so advanced that models designed for automated IR survey of PV plants “out of the box” are now available [73] for less than $30,000. For these reasons drone inspections are standard operating procedure by multiple large PV developers/operators.

In comparison, ground robots for PV plant inspection are technically and commercially immature. As noted, several models exist but they are all essentially in field testing by the manufacturer or clients, and not deployed in standard operations. However the pace and opportunity for technical development are great: Because robots can carry much equipment and approach close to subjects, they offer the possibility of high-resolution and sophisticated imaging of subjects, for example capturing visual, IR and PL images of an under-performing module. It also appears technically feasible that in the future robots could operate fully autonomously, i.e. with no operator or even communication with a mission-control base. The goal is that all functions and decisions are performed “on the edge”, i.e. by the robot system itself, including navigation, obstacle avoidance, image analysis, fault categorisation, and obtaining further imaging of detected faults.

An alternative approach to drones and robots for increasing efficiency of solar-farm inspection, described by an inspection service provider in Australia, is to mount camera(s) to a utility vehicle and drive between PV rows, recording high-resolution images continually and rapidly. The images are later processed by computer, using machine learning to identify faults. Key advantages of this approach are: utility vehicles are usually already on hand at solar farms, hence the only additional capital expenditure is for the cameras. Such vehicles can cope with harsh terrain and they drive faster than robots. However at present there is still much human involvement in the image collection and analysis procedures.

Overall, it appears that drones will continue to be the dominant tool for visual and IR inspection of PV modules on solar farms for the foreseeable future, because of their high efficiency and technical and commercial maturity. They are already used commercially at some largescale PV plants, and with “out of the box” IR survey drones now available, we expect their use will grow further. Ground robots are far less mature but they promise unique and valuable capabilities such as sophisticated module imaging with high quality and new methods, thermal inspection of site electrics for fire safety, and fully autonomous operation. In situations where drones can be readily flown and the sole task is to localize faulty PV modules and strings, ground robots may not be needed. Where use of drones is restricted, or the goal is to autonomously detect a wide variety of solar farm issues, robots appear promising.

## **7. Conclusions**

This study reviewed the status and potential of ground robots for solar farm inspection. Especially they are compared to drones inspection technology, which is fully commercialised and used in routine operations at some solar farms. Because the cost of drones continues to fall while their capabilities and ease-of-use increase, and they are very fast at

collecting images, aerial inspection appears likely to become even more common. However drones have certain constraints, especially their use is limited by regulations in many areas, and they do not see the back side of PV modules or balance-of-system (BOS) items such as electrical connectors and cables. Thermal inspection of BOS items is important for safety as they are the primary source of fires in PV plants.

Robots have the potential to fulfil this need for autonomous, groundlevel inspection of PV plants. We reviewed 36 mobile inspection robots available in the market in mid 2024, of which six were specifically designed for solar farms or had been regularly adapted for that purpose. Their development stage can be summarised as “proof of performance” — they are generally in field testing at a small number of sites, and PV plant owners/operators have not yet incorporated them into standard O&M procedures, unlike drone inspection.

Interestingly, a variety of robot locomotion types has been adopted. Of the six dedicated PV inspection robots, three used tracks, two wheels, and one legs. In general legs tend to be the most agile but are relatively inefficient, complex and expensive; tracks are well suited to rough and soft terrain; and wheels are the most efficient and simple mechanism but require relatively smooth and firm ground.

Naturally, the choice of robot locomotion for solar farm inspection depends on typical ground conditions. We investigated terrains of solar farms across Australia, visiting six sites and interviewing industry contacts about conditions at other sites across the country. In summary the main obstacles were: (i) vegetation, with solar farms in all regions except deserts requiring regular mowing, (ii) pools of water and mud after rain, especially where drainage is poor, (iii) ditches caused by soil erosion at newly-built sites and in high-rainfall areas. Linkage bars between tracker rows and above-ground cable trays were rare, but when used created a hard obstacle to robots as well as regular maintenance vehicles. Overall, we assessed that solar farms in moderately dry locations, i. e. infrequent pools of water and minor erosion ditches, could deploy efficient wheeled robots, while tracked robots may be needed in wetter locations. Legged robots appear less suitable at present as they are relatively expensive, complex and have shorter travel distances.

The greatest potential for inspection robots stems from their relative strengths: “seeing” at ground level, carrying heavy payloads, and remaining stationary during imaging. As well as thermal BOS and module rear-side inspections mentioned, robots appear especially suited to high-quality and comprehensive investigation of PV defects. For example, in principle they could (i) deploy several different imaging technologies simultaneously, e.g. visual, IR and PL, (ii) approach close to subjects for high resolution, and (iii) take long-duration images (exposure time or many repetitions) for advanced techniques such as PL. Another opportunity for robots is to incorporate other solar farm O&M tasks such as security monitoring, module installation verification and even mowing weeds — all of which have already been pursued by robot manufacturers. Finally, robots have the potential to become fully autonomous, unlike drones where a human operator remains mandatory so far, which is attractive for remote locations, worker safety, and labour cost.

In conclusion, autonomous robotic inspection of solar farms is an emerging technology which appears likely to complement, not replace, aerial drone surveys. Robots are especially suited to detecting hot spots in PV electrical systems – valuable for fire safety – and acquiring detailed and advanced images of PV faults. Fast and efficient wheeled robots appear adequate for moderately dry and smooth sites, while tracked locomotion can cope with rougher terrain and has been adopted by most dedicated PV inspection robots so far.
